blocks.html: Getting Started with Claude. This is Claude 101, built from a live OneAccord session, Building AI-Native Ways of Working. Watch the recording, read the short teaching sections (they confirm the key ideas and correct or update a few things said on the call), answer a knowledge check, then respond to a scenario. Your coach grades it, and 3 of 4 points passes.

blocks.title: Building AI-Native Ways of Working: Getting Started with Claude

blocks.note: Heads up: the recording was made in August 2026 and the automatic transcript garbles some words. Where you see or hear "Clark" or "cloud", it means Claude, and "Oasis" means OASYS. A few points on the call are also refined in the sections below, so treat this text as the current version.

blocks.html:
1. What "AI-native" means

An AI-native organization hands the mundane, repetitive work to AI so people can do what only people can do: judgment, creativity, expertise and client relationships. The payoff is more time, more energy and better margin, for OneAccord and for your own consulting practice.

AI-native does not mean replacing people. You stay accountable for everything that goes to a client.

Three quick wins most people start with: drafting emails, meeting summaries (record your Teams calls and let AI capture the notes so you can focus on the client), and restructuring docs and decks.

2. Prompting fundamentals

  • Goal: say exactly what you want from Claude and in what form ("give me 10 LinkedIn post ideas", "help me think this through").
  • Context: give everything you know: the client, the tool, what's been tried, your hunch. Speak it with the microphone; you'll get your full train of thought in quickly, and Claude works out mis-transcribed words from context.
  • Let Claude ask questions: Claude often asks 3 to 5 clarifying questions on its own. If a tool jumps straight to answers, tell it: "Ask me questions first."

A useful shortcut is the WE framework: Who are we? (who you are and the role Claude should play, such as a seasoned editor) and How do we get what we want? (the specific task plus the victory outcome, so the work aims at a bullseye and not just an activity).

If an answer misses, don't give up on AI. Correct it: "that's not what I asked for", "that's wrong because…", or add more information. Sharing an example of a past workflow also cuts the number of rounds a lot.

Tip: when you're still working out requirements, say "Don't build anything yet". Otherwise Claude may start producing a deliverable you'll change in the next message, which wastes credits.

3. Projects vs. skills

This was the most-asked question on the call, so here is the clean version.

ProjectSkill
What it isA workspace for one client, offering or initiativeA repeatable process or framework Claude follows the same way every time
HoldsKnowledge files, instructions, chat history, memoryStep-by-step instructions, templates and reference files
When Claude uses itAlways, for every chat in that projectOn demand, in any chat or project, when it's relevant or you call it
ExamplesA client engagement; building the OASYS offeringOA brand kit, OA documents, CSP process, SOP builder, a RACI framework, the sales coach

Rule of thumb: if it's context about one thing, use a project. If it's a process you'll reuse on many things, make it a skill. They work best together: a client project supplies the context, and skills supply the how ("use the CSP skill on this client", "brand this with the OA brand kit").

Practical notes:

  • Start a new project by asking Claude to help you write the project instructions.
  • A document created inside a project is not saved to its knowledge base automatically. Add final versions deliberately, and leave drafts out.
  • Skills are editable. After using one, ask Claude to review how the work went and suggest updates. To build one, just say "I need to create a Claude skill for…" and the built-in skill creator takes over.
  • Skills shared across the company keep everyone on one version. Sending copies around creates version-control problems, so ask before circulating files.

4. Connectors and Claude inside Microsoft 365

A connector gives Claude permission to read, and sometimes update, the tools you already use: Outlook email, SharePoint, Notion, Slack, Granola call transcripts and hundreds more. Instead of copying and pasting between tools, you say "pull the transcript from my call with…and add the to-dos to Notion."

Two clarifications on what was said in the session:

  • Claude is also available inside Excel, Word, PowerPoint and Outlook as add-ins (installed from the Microsoft Marketplace) on a paid Claude plan. On Team and Enterprise plans an organization owner must switch on cross-app use first.
  • Claude in Chrome is a browser extension, not a connector in the strict sense. It can research a site and fill in forms for you while you watch. It will pause when you need to step in, for example to pay.

Not sure whether something connects? Ask Claude. "Do you have a connector for this tool?" is a perfectly good question.

5. Protect client data and verify everything

The call said "the paid account is the secure account." That's a good instinct but too simple. The accurate version:

  • Use OneAccord's company Claude account for client work and follow the OneAccord AI use policy.
  • Personal Free, Pro and Max accounts have a setting that lets your chats be used to improve the model, and it's up to each user. So a paid personal plan is not automatically safe for client data. Business plans (Team and Enterprise) are governed by commercial terms and are handled separately.
  • On any other AI tool, especially a free one, don't paste client information until you've confirmed its data-training settings. If in doubt, ask before you share.
  • Keep work and personal chats separate. Claude builds memory from your conversations, so keeping the work account for work keeps its context clean and relevant.

Recording calls: recording every client and sales call is the OneAccord standard, and Teams shows a recording notice to participants. Make sure clients know they're being recorded, and check the AI use policy if you're unsure.

Never send anything you haven't read. You still verify accuracy before it goes to a client. The goal is for the human to do only what a human should do, not to skip the human.

blocks.prompt: In your own words, which best describes an AI-native organization?
options: One that replaces consultants with AI agents wherever possible
One that hands repetitive, mundane work to AI so people focus on judgment, creativity, expertise and client relationships
One that uses AI only for drafting emails
One that lets each person use any AI tool with any client data
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Right. AI takes the mundane work; people bring judgment and expertise, and that builds margin.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite. AI-native means AI handles the mundane work so people can focus on what only humans can do.

blocks.prompt: You're about to ask Claude for help with a tricky client problem. Which prompt approach works best?
options: A one-line question, then judge the answer
State the goal, then give full context by speaking it, and let Claude ask clarifying questions
Ask for the final deliverable right away and edit it afterward
Copy your last prompt from a different task
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Exactly. Goal plus rich context plus letting Claude ask questions gets much better results.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Better: state the goal, give full context (speaking it is fastest), and let Claude ask clarifying questions.

blocks.prompt: You're gathering requirements for a new deliverable and Claude keeps starting to build it. What should you say?
options: Nothing, just let it finish and redo it later
"Don't build anything yet. Ask me questions first until we have the full picture."
Start a brand-new account
Switch to a shorter prompt
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Right. Holding off the build until requirements are clear saves time and credits.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Tell Claude not to build yet and to ask questions first. Otherwise it rebuilds every time you add instructions.

blocks.prompt: You have a OneAccord brand kit you want to use on every client deliverable, in any project. Where should it live?
options: A project, because it's about OneAccord
A skill, because it's a reusable process Claude can use anywhere
A SharePoint template library nobody opens
It doesn't need to be saved
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Reusable across many things means a skill.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: It should be a skill. Skills are reusable across projects and chats; projects hold context about one thing.

blocks.prompt: You're working with one specific client and want Claude to remember their documents, history and instructions for every chat about them. What fits best?
options: A project for that client
A skill for that client
Only a saved email
A free personal account
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Right. A project keeps one client's context together and always available.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: That's a project: a workspace of context for one client, always loaded for chats inside it.

blocks.prompt: You created a final proposal inside a client project. What's true about the project's knowledge base?
options: It's saved there automatically
It's saved only if you deliberately add it
Claude deletes it after a week
Only drafts are saved
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Add finished documents to the knowledge base on purpose, and leave drafts out.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Documents created in a project aren't added to the knowledge base automatically. Add final versions deliberately.

blocks.prompt: Which statement about protecting client data is the most accurate?
options: Any paid AI account is safe for client data
Use the OneAccord company account, follow the AI use policy, and check data-training settings before putting client information into any other tool
Free accounts are fine if you delete the chat afterward
Client data is safe in any tool as long as it's for work
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Right. The company account and the AI use policy come first, and other tools need a check.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Paid doesn't automatically mean safe. Use the company account, follow the AI use policy, and check settings before sharing client data elsewhere.

blocks.prompt: Claude drafted a client-ready deck for you and it looks great. What now?
options: Send it: Claude is accurate
Read it through and verify it before it goes to the client
Ask a colleague to send it
Ask Claude to send it without review
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Exactly. You stay accountable, so read it and verify it first.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Always review and verify. AI does the busy work; you are still responsible for the result.

blocks.promptHtml:
A client tells you: "I tried AI and I don't like it. It never gives me good answers." They also mention they paste a few client spreadsheets into a free AI tool on their phone.

Write how you'd respond. Explain what you'd suggest they change and how you'd handle the data concern.
rubric: Suggests better prompting: a clear goal and lots of context (ideally spoken), and inviting the AI to ask clarifying questions
Says to correct or refine weak answers by adding information instead of giving up, or mentions giving examples
Raises the data concern: don't put client data in a free or unvetted tool; use a business account and check data-training settings and policy
Reinforces that a person still reviews and verifies AI output before relying on it or sending it

Consumer plans (Free, Pro, Max) can be used for model improvement if the user opts in, so a paid personal plan is not automatically 'secure'. Keep work and personal chats separate.
